utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today, we are Monday, the 27th of October, 2008. Let me greet the Prosecution team, Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom. As you know, today we are starting at 9.00. We will run until 12.00 and have a 20-minute break around 10.15, and resume again at 1.00 until 4.00, and we will have a break around quarter past 2.00. So much for today's agenda. I believe the Registrar has a few IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through witness Simunovic, Marinko. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number 1C 00870. The list submitted as 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00871. The list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit number IC 00872. Petkovic Defence team has submitted correction of the list of exhibits tendered through witness Zelenika, Mirko which was given Exhibit number IC 00866. This correction shall be given Exhibit number IC 00873. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. On line 24, page 1, the numbers have not been recorded. Could you check, Registrar, please, on the transcript. It seems that a few IC numbers are missing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can repeat exhibit numbers. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00870.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Could you give me your first name, last name, and date the birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neven Tomic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can no longer hear the speaker. There's too much background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Could you give me your date of birth again, please, your first name, last name and date the birth. This has not been recorded. Please speak louder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neven Tomic, born on the 21st of April, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told me that you had a degree. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently, I work at my own company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this firm is involved in what business sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The IT industry; software, computer science.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before a court of law regarding those events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or are you testifying for the first time today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down. Just some information I'd like to convey to you about the way in which these proceedings will unfold. Mr. Karnavas, whom I'm sure you've met over the weekend, has mentioned this to you already. You shall have to answer questions which will be put to you by Mr. Prlic's counsel, Mr. Karnavas; and Mr. Karnavas will also show you a series of documents which are contained in a binder, which I'm sure you have seen already; and I'm sure you have seen each document together with him. After this stage, which will take at least two days, I am sure, the Defence counsel of the other accused will put questions to you as part of their cross-examination or examination-in-chief, if they address topics which have not been addressed by Mr. Karnavas' examination. Once this is over, the Prosecution, who is sitting on your right-hand side, will then cross-examine you for the same time as Mr. Karnavas has had. The Bench, comprising the three Judges in front of you, may also put questions to you, once we have the documents in front of us. This will depend on the subject, and this will be on a case-by-case basis. As Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Prlic's Defence counsel, has planned to hear you for quite a long time, there's every chance you will still be here next Monday and next Tuesday, according to the schedule we've been given. You have taken the solemn declaration, which means that from now onwards you are a witness of the Court and you may no longer contact Mr. Karnavas. Please try and be as accurate as you possibly can when you answer these questions. If you don't understand a question, please do not hesitate to ask the person who has put the question to rephrase it. We theoretically have breaks every hour and a half, but today we shall have a shorter break, since we will finish at 12.00 today, resume again at 1.00, and run until 4.00. However, tomorrow we will start our hearing in the morning, and until Thursday we will be sitting in the morning. If at any point in time you to not feel well, please to not hesitate to let us know so that we can suspend the hearing. It is extremely tiring to answer questions relentlessly, and it can be an ordeal for any witness, particularly when it lasts a long time. If you don't feel well at any point in time, please do not hesitate and let us know. The Trial Chamber is, of course, entirely prepared to answer any of your questions. This is what I wanted to share with you to make sure that these proceedings unfold as smoothly as possible, in the interests of this trial and in the interests of justice in general. Mr. Karnavas, I'm happy to give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom, and good morning especially to you, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have to speak a little louder so we can capture every word. I'm going to ask you to speak slowly. Before I begin, Your Honours, I should note last night we did file a supplemental with a list of documents that were presented by Mr. Tomic, some 54 documents. Of those, only three will be used, and I'm told that I should point that out in advance so they can be released in the e-court. They're 1D 03046, 1D 03050 and 1D 03051. They're -- each document is two or three pages. So, anyway, I point that out, Your Honours. So with your permission, if they can be released into e-court. As for the other documents, we will be filing a motion to add them on to the 65 ter list. They have not been translated. Only four of the fifty-four documents were translated over the weekend. Now, with that -- I need a decision, Your Honour. Perhaps you guys -- Your Honours can confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, after having deliberated, authorises you to add these documents to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, let me begin by asking you a little bit about your background. I understand you're from the Mostar area and you studied in Mostar, obtaining a degree in Economics from the University of Mostar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in what year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Picking up from there, if you could just briefly, very briefly, tell us about your work background from 1980 all the way until, say, 1990, when the first elections occurred, or 1991.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: After graduating from university, I started working at a company called Unis Elektronik in Mostar as an economist, in the sales department and in the economic analysis department. In 1985, I became a professional politician, as the president of the youth organisation of Mostar. That was one of the political organisations in the former system. After that, in 1987, I became the director of the revenues department, and basically, ex officio, a member of the city government, the executive council of the city of Mostar. During a certain period of time, I was acting head of finance because for a while there wasn't an elected head, so it was the municipal budget that I took care of. While I was head of the revenues department or taxation department, the 1990 elections took place, and when the following parties won, the SDA, the HDZ and the SDS; and then it was the SDS that was supposed to get the position as the head of the taxation department, and therefore, I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's go back a little bit. With respect to you being the president of the youth organisation for the Mostar municipality, could you just very briefly tell us what did that entail, because as I understand it, that was a professional position for one year.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did that on a professional basis. The youth organisation brought together all the young people up to the age of 27, up to the age of 27, I say; and it represented a form of political organisation in the former Yugoslavia. There was the League of Communists, the Veterans organisation, the trade unions' organisation, the Socialist Alliance of the Working People, so the youth organisation was one of these political organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to speak a little slower. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to speak a little slower. Otherwise, our interpreters are not going to make it through the morning. All right. Now, with respect to -- in 1987, it was translated that you were the director of the revenue department. We're talking about the tax department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the director of the revenues department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us, what did that department do and what did you do concretely?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: In the former system, there were two institutions that collected public revenues. One was the SDK, the public accounting service that collected revenues from the companies, enterprises, by way of checking their accounts and carrying out appropriate legislation. And the second institution that was organised at the municipal level was in charge of collecting revenues for municipal budgets from the private sector at the time; that is to say, from farmers, butchers, caterers, restauranteurs, small-scale enterprises that did not have the status of real companies at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if I understand it, even prior to the 1990 elections there was some form of private enterprise, albeit for small businesses, in the former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in that particular department, how many employees were there besides yourself, as the director?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Around 60 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as I indicated -- as you indicated, after the 1990 elections that position was allocated, that is, the director of the revenue or tax department, was allocated to somebody from the SDA.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: [In English] SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: SDS party, and I take it you were out of a job because of that.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So let's pick it up from there. What did you do? You're out of a job. It's 1990. What happens?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: At the time, I did not want to run in the elections, although I had received an offer or, rather, offers from several parties; namely, the Liberal Party that had been established by the former youth organisation, then the SDP, the former Communist Party that was the successor of the League of Communists, and the Green Party in Mostar that I had established together with my friends. At the time, I had contacts with some people from the HDZ as well, primarily those people who worked in the municipal organs. I had good relations with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just speed it up a little bit. What kind of work did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I have to point out that when the new executive council was elected, a great step backwards was made in terms of the competence of the elected people to carry out that particular work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: That was the first distribution of positions after they had won power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Distributions by the political parties?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the political parties gave these positions to their own people. However, they had had no experience in running a municipal administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did that cause any problems?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Of course it did, because after the very first month, they ran into great difficulties, like the problem of getting the garbage out of town, then carrying out tax reforms, the problem of illegal construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you could just tell us, what was the next position that you held?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Six months later, I was made an offer to be the director of the fund for the construction and development of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what did that entail, specifically?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: That fund was the successor of the former socialist self-management community of interest that had run the town and town planning, as such, that was in charge of the financing of town planning, that collected money from rent, that is to say, on the basis of what had already been invested in infrastructure. Then we financed the building of new infrastructure, that is to say, municipal roads, streets, waterworks, sewage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you have to join a political party in order to receive that position?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: There were pressures brought to bear for me to join the HDZ and to sign an application form. However, I didn't do that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long did you hold this position?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I held that position until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then what did you do in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Then we left the premises that were in the eastern part of town, because it became impossible to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Tomic, you know, you went from speaking very fast to very slow, and it's almost difficult for the interpreters to do it word for word because they are highly competent. So if you to so, a medium, full sentence, trust me, they are terrific people. All right. Now, you said you had to leave the east side. Why was that? And if you could tell us, what was located on the east side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: In the eastern part of town, there were the premises of all administrative bodies; the Municipal Administration, my fund, the mayor's office, the Defence Department. Only the Secretariat of the Interior was in the western part of town. At the time, the reserve units of the JNA were already in town. The first confrontations began. Fear was spreading. People were afraid of going to work and even staying in Mostar, especially in early April, when a tanker truck exploded. Many inhabitants left town then, and many institutions could not work properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall about when that explosion took place and where, which month? You know, we could --

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: It was in early April, and the explosion was immediately -- in the immediate vicinity of the barracks, the so-called northern camp. I don't know that -- after the explosion, I took my children and my sister children -- my sister's children and my parents to Makarska. Many citizens did that. It was mostly women and children who left and became refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us that a lot of the administrative offices were on the east side. What about the SDK and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas. I would like to talk a bit more about the explosion of the truck. You've just stated, Witness, that you took your family to Makarska, but that you were not the only one and that many people did the same. I'm rather surprised to hear this. If this was an accidental explosion, indeed there was no reason to be alarmed, but if it was a criminal explosion, then it was different. So according to you, what was the cause of this explosion? Was it just an accident or was it a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody knew at the moment of the explosion, no one of my co-workers knew that. There were various statements. Various statements could be heard, some saying that the incident had been staged by the JNA themselves to produce chaos, or, on the other hand, that it was -- it happened by chance or, alternatively, that it was a criminal act, et cetera. But tension was present in the city at the time, and people were starting to leave the city, mostly women and children. The explosion only speeded up the process and turned it into a chaotic evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Since we're on this issue, I'll ask my follow-up question now. Now, you said a lot of women and children left. Were these women housewives or did they also work -- have working positions? And if so, do you know where they would have been working?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking mostly about mothers with children. Some were housewives, others had employment. Out of the six women that worked at my fund, four left, so that the fund could no longer function. And that was the situation in many other institutions too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I -- the SDK, was it located on the east side or the west side?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: On the east side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for cutting you off, Mr. Karnavas, but I'm very surprised to hear you say that out of six women working in your department, four left. And you said that the same happened in other business sectors and other institutions. Were these people leaving spontaneously because they were afraid or did people leave following instructions telling them to leave? Are we talking here about individual decisions to leave or did people respond to instructions given by X, Y, Z?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The motivation was exclusively fear, because in Mostar there had already been assassinations, shootings, et cetera, so people were afraid for themselves and their children. Those who had relatives in the Western Herzegovina or who were originally from there went there or others went to the Adriatic coast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at this history of your town, the history of Mostar, can we find similar situations in the past where the population was afraid and left the city because of that or is it something that was unprecedented, because it's a rare occurrence to see the population of a city leave the city because they're afraid. When such things happen, it's because serious things are going on. Had this already happened in the history of Mostar or not? Is it something that had occurred before or not, these people leaving because they were afraid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, people were leaving for reasons of fear exclusively. There was no organisation in place. I don't know whether anything similar had happened in -- before in history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's move rather quickly into your involvement in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, as some point you were involved with the Crisis Staff. If you could tell us a little bit about that. What was the Crisis Staff and how did you get involved in it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: At that time in April, when the institutions stopped working one after the other, my fund included, I cooperated with Mr. Gagro, the mayor; and on April the 20th, Mr. Kazazic, my colleague who worked at the housing maintenance fund, which is a similar organisation to mine, or was, we went to the Crisis Staff, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir, so you need to pick it up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we went to the Crisis Staff and we said to them that we were at their disposal. We wanted to assist in the organisation of the financial system at those times. The Crisis Staff had its premises in the basement of the director's [as interpreted] office. Organisationally speaking or with regard to the organisation of the city, it was not competent. People who were supposed to work in the sector of finance had no experience whatsoever. And then Mr. Kazazic and I were appointed to work on financial issues, and we were to have relations with the SDK. We immediately drafted two decrees, signed by the Crisis Staff, and we also drafted instructions, but it was too late already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A point regarding the transcript. On page 15, line 6, we read "director's office," but I think it was the rectorate's office, the office of the president of the university, and I think that is misleading if it's left like this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this gentleman that you were working with, concretely, what did you do with him during that period of time? And if you could tell us what the period is. What period are we talking about? This would be late April to what period?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the period starting on April the 21st, and it was our task to try and raise money for the citizens, because at the time we were out of cash. There were no more Yugoslav dinars left. And that's why we had prepared such a decree, which was then published by the Crisis Staff about the -- about limitations to -- for the use of cash and cheques and the like, and those are decrees that are commonly issued in the early days of a crisis. But the Crisis Staff failed to publish these in a timely fashion. However, a few days after these decrees, it was no longer possible to even go to the SDK, and the last people who had been there said that the safe had been broken open by the JNA reserve units and that there was money lying around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before I go into the next topic, which would be the special-purpose council which we all know that you were involved in, perhaps this would be a good time for you to give us a brief explanation of how the SDK functioned.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The SDK was a public institution before the war. It was organised by Belgrade as the federal SDK. Then every republic had its own SDK. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the SDK headquarters was in Sarajevo, or the head office, and all economic analyses were made there, accounts were checked, payment was -- payment was checked, et cetera, and there were also regional branch offices. Mostar was the branch office for all of Herzegovina, from Trebinje to Livno; and there were also lower-level offices in the municipalities, or branches in the municipalities. So all institutions, all companies, were required to have an account with the SDK, and they had to deposit cash there. And all their payment would also go exclusively through the SDK. The SDK collected taxes and contributions for funding public expenditures. They also carried out some -- they had some control functions. And I must say that at municipal level, this institution was independent from the municipal authorities, so that the Municipal Assembly could not give instructions to the SDK to raise additional taxes and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us that the SDK offices were on the east side. You've told us that the situation is rather grave in Mostar. This is around April 1992. Could you please describe to us whether at this point in time, that is, late April or early May, whether the SDK, the regional branch in Mostar, whether it is functioning, and to what extent, if it is?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Very few people had remained at the SDK. Most of them worked as security officers. The operations had ceased in late April because communications had been interrupted, and the SDK cannot work without telecommunications; so they couldn't communicate with the head office in Sarajevo, so that their activity was reduced exclusively to payments within Mostar and cash operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about the administration, the tax administration that you had worked for? I take it they were collecting taxes from small businesses. Did they have cash on hand, and more specifically, was that administration working at that point in time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: That administration dissolved because the director had left Mostar for Eastern Herzegovina, and the Crisis Staff did not appoint another person, and the secretary of finances, who was a member of the Crisis Staff, was incompetent, a person who hadn't worked in that area, so that the service didn't function at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just if you could tell us, do you know what area had he worked in before he was appointed by virtue of his membership into the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he had worked for a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we understand, because we've seen documents and heard testimony, that at one point in time you became involved in what is known as the special-purpose council. So before we talk about your specific involvement, if you could briefly describe to us, so we have some context, how the situation is in Mostar. So this would be around mid-May or so. What is the situation in Mostar specifically with respect to the various administrative departments in Mostar, whether they're functioning, to what extent, because we do know that we have a Crisis Staff, but -- you know, but we need to know to what extent the city is functioning, or the municipality.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: First of all, I can say that the city and its institutions did not function. The Crisis Staff -- it was up to the Crisis Staff to make sure that some services functioned at times of war, but those services were no established, so that it was all left to the individual initiative. It was all left to individual initiatives. There were people who previously had been responsible, directors of companies or institutions, who went to the Crisis Staff and volunteered to work. It was their intention to make themselves useful, to make use of their business relations, in order to help the citizens of Mostar. Those activities go back to the time when Dubrovnik was shelled, when aid was collected for Dubrovnik, and those people would occasionally have informal meetings with Mayor Gagro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here for one second. What period are we talking about with respect to aiding Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: It was in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And to what extent were these individuals trying to assist in providing aid to Dubrovnik, and to what extent was Mr. Gagro involved?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: He was to provide contacts where the trucks [Realtime transcript read in error, "Turks"] should go, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you involved in any way during that effort?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. This information, he was to provide contacts where the "Turks" should go, is not quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can explain, if it is not a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is a mistake in the transcript. I heard "trucks" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- but I was going to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You said "trucks"?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, stepping back, you said the Crisis Staff wasn't functioning and certain services were supposed to be established. Perhaps you could clarify that. Which services were to be established by the Crisis Staff that were not established?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The city of Mostar and all the other municipalities had the municipal defence plans in place, and this plan envisaged quite clearly what organs, what institutions, should continue functioning if there was a war or an imminent threat of war. What the plan did not envisage was that the Yugoslav People's Army would actually carry out the attack. In those plans, it was always foreseen that the attacks would come either from Italy or from Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Stop. So that's why, you know, the blue helmets or the red helmets?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Blue being the Western powers, red being the Soviets and the satellites?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So those plans were not usable in their entirety, but it was because of the incompetence of the people in the Staff. They were not adapted to the existing situation, so that the former Territorial Defence Staff was not operational, the Income Administration was not functioning, the Urban Planning Secretariat was not operational. It was very important in terms of municipal services, utilities, such as the municipal waste collection, water supply, all those municipal activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you did indicate that you had been assisting the Crisis Staff with Mr. Kazazic, but I take it you were not a member of the Crisis Staff but you were merely assisting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were in charge of this area because the head of finances was formally a member of the Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, to your knowledge, did you ever see these -- the municipal defence plans? Has Mr. Gagro, as the head of the Crisis Staff, ever bring out the municipal defence plans to see how, to any extent, they might be adjusted to the unfolding circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to see those plans while I was in the executive board, before the elections, because as the director of the Income Administration, I did have some obligations that had to do with the drafting of those plans. However, Mr. Gagro did not ask me anything about those plans, nor was this a topic of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just to make sure that we all understand, this is during the Yugoslavian period, sort of 1987 to 1990, when you were working for the Department of Taxation; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I was in charge, that was the term that was used, of the defence plan, the segments of that plan that had to do with tax revenue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And your situation was not unique. I take it that in -- or was it unique? Did the other heads of departments, whether it's SDK or other municipal administrations, were they also responsible for knowing what's in the defence plan; for their sectors, that is?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Of course, everybody had a role according to the defence plan. Some sectors would cease to work under that plan. Some bigger sectors would be set up. Some functions no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, if that was the case, could you please explain to us, perhaps if you know, why it was Mr. Gagro didn't activate the defence plan? Are we to assume that he wasn't aware that such plans existed?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to your involvement with the special-purpose council. If you could please tell us, because we know -- we've seen documents that you were part of this special-purpose council, if you could please explain to us, first of all, how was it that you became a member, and then tell us, to your understanding, what was the special-purpose council about, what was its functions?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, throughout the time, and this is why I started talking about the period when Dubrovnik was shelled, throughout the time that the Crisis Staff existed some of the competent people, managers of companies, directors of institutions, were trying to find a way how to help; and we started getting together. The manager of the Mostar Privredna Banka bank, Mr. Vegar, even provided us with an office in a building that belonged to this bank; and we would go there and we would talk and discuss about ways in which we could help. Some of these people went to the Crisis Staff and offered various things, from the food that they had in their warehouses, the liabilities that they had -- or, rather, the assets that they had, that they had to collect from other companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was this an executive administration? Did it have any executive authority, this special-purpose council, while you were a member of it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I would like to say this: The council was appointed by the Municipal HVO Staff, and that's when it was given this form of a council. And the reason why this was necessary was primarily because it made it possible for the council members to travel around in the performance of their job. We did not have any executive power. We did not decide on any issues that were within the purview of the municipal administration. The only thing was to create conditions for the assistance and aid to reach the citizens of Mostar and to protect the property of the companies that had their seats in Mostar located abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But as I understand it, and we'll get to a document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll get to a document very shortly, but as I understand it, you, among two others, were designated as a coordinator, and can you please explain to the Trial Chamber and to the rest of us what exactly this position entailed as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, like any other coordinator, since the members were on the road, one of the coordinators always had to be present there because the council members had to ensure they had vehicles, "lesse passe," so this was purely to coordinate activities for the implementation of the tasks that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry to interrupt. Witness, you said that the council did not have any executive power, unlike the municipal organs. However, this council had to protect the property of companies, but how, because you didn't have any powers, so how was it supposed to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you an example, using the Soko company in Mostar as an example. It manufactured parts for Dornier and other aircraft industries in Europe. They had money in their bank accounts in Frankfurt. They received the money for the goods that they had delivered to Germany. The Soko management, headed by the general manager, went to Belgrade, and they issued an order from Belgrade that this money should be spent, because up until that time they had the authority to sign off things like that. And we, as the council, contacted the people from Soko, the deputy manager, because he was still there, and we sent them to Germany to explain the situation to the people there, what the situation was like in Soko, and to put a stop to the expenditure of this money. And the German partner really did put a stop to the payments and even offered to take on 18 workers from Soko. They were to be given jobs in Germany. So this was -- and also they provided an ambulance car. It was their donation. So you can see now that a member of the council went up there, and he did all that. He protected the property of a company from Mostar, prevented this money from being spent, and he also got this ambulance van by way of a donation. So this had nothing to do with any kind of administrative work, any kind of administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If there are no other questions, I'll -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you could please tell us, how long were you with the special-purpose council, up until what point in time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I was with the council up until the time when I was appointed the head of the finance office. That's the 15th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So -- well, before we move on to that segment, perhaps we can look at some documents dealing with the special-purpose council. So if you could look at your binder, and I'm going to be referring to three documents in particular. The first one is 1D 03050. 1D 03050. This is dated 21 April 1992. Sir, are you familiar with this document, and if so, could you please tell us how?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document because I drafted it together with my colleague, Mr. Kazazic. It's an instruction on the implementation of the order on the use of cash, because we had run out of cash, and this was an attempt on our part to use accounts cheques and other forms of payment as much as possible because there simply was no cash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you can see that this document does make reference to the public accounting services, the SDK, and during this period of time can you confirm to us whether it was working as it had been in the past, that is, connected to Sarajevo and to the rest of the country, or had the SDK been impaired by this point?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: In that period, the communications with Sarajevo were down. I think that in early April, a truck with cash was stopped in Konjic because there were roadblocks set up there, and after the telecommunication lines went down it was impossible to use those, so the SDK could operate only partially in the Mostar area to effect payments within companies in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that we're supposed to break at 10.15. If I could go on for a few more minutes, I can close this chapter up. Two brief documents, Your Honour, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document is 1D 02389. 1D 02389. And this is dated May 1992, and this is a decision to appoint you and others to the special-purpose council. You see that, sir, do you not? Do you have the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see your name here at the very top; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the last paragraph, number 4, we see that you are to be one of the coordinators, along with Mr. Prlic and Mr. Puljic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, in this capacity -- well, let me just ask you this: Since you were the coordinator, along with Mr. Prlic and Mr. Puljic, did you have -- did you exercise any authority over the other members of the special-purpose council?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: No authority in terms of subordination. It was simply coordination of activities, so that you don't have three people visit the same institution in the same village, because there were no vehicles, no fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could look at the next document, which is 1D 03051, 1D 03051, we see this is dated 6th June 1992, and there seems to be two signatures on the special-purpose council coordinators. Have you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we can see from the very first paragraph that it says that this report covers the activities of certain members, and it mentions Slezak, Salahovic, Primorac and Orucevic. Did you know these gentlemen and could you confirm to us that they were also involved in the special-purpose council?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we can see briefly some of the activities. Do you know whether, in fact, this report is consistent with what you were able to observe at the time, that it talks about the field of payment, telecommunications or communications, there's a list of other activities, humanitarian aid? We see that there are current activities.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, this corresponds to the kind of activities that we had at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at the very last page of this document, and I'm going to focus our attention to the last two paragraphs, primarily, starting with the second-to-last paragraph, it says here: "Besides the mention of concrete activities, some members of the council were intensely engaged in the forming of HVO Mostar war government, especially in the preparation of appropriate acts on the establishing and defining of activities of the town civilian authorities," and so on and so forth. Do you know what this is referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. We had prepared two documents as part of our activities. People with experience in administration, such as Mr. Prlic, Puljic, Kozul, Jahic, Kazazic; so we had drafted a document about what the war government should look like, with a description of the relevant purviews. That was based mostly on our knowledge of how government functioned and on the previous defence plans, and we put this in the form of a proposal to Mr. Topic. And we also submitted a proposal containing the list of regulations that this government should enact in order for life to be organised. These were mostly activities that were envisaged in the defence plans that we had been familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And finally, if we look at the very last paragraph, a meeting is suggested between members of the council and the president of the Croatian Defence Council in order to define the status of the special-purpose council and its tasks, as well as its composition and form for the upcoming period. Do you know whether, in fact, such a meeting took place? And if so, what, if any, outcomes came about from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, the municipal HVO had already been appointed, and the first decisions had already been issued, inter alia, about the establishment of the office in charge of providing supplies to the town, the finance department, and we thought that some of the activities of the council could now be transferred back to those institutions and that the members of the council could go back to their companies and try to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, we could take that break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Unless there are any questions regarding the special-purpose council, I'm going to move on. Seeing no questions from the Bench, let me fast forward a little bit, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Briefly, I want you to discuss with us your involvement with the HVO HZ-HB. That's the executive authority of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And we've seen documents. We know at one point you were appointed, as you had indicated earlier, as the head of the finance department. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct, in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could please tell us, describe to us, in your understanding what was the HVO HZ-HB, this executive authority? What was its function?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Our function was to organise life in the territory where the HVO was in charge of defence, as the military structure concerned. So it was the organisation of civilian life and assistance in terms of defence. That was the basic task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we have also heard some testimony concerning the various positions and how it operated, and that this was a collective body. Can you confirm whether, indeed, the HVO HZ-HB acted as a collective body?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As such, could you please tell us whether the president of the HVO HZ-HB, that would be Dr. Jadranko Prlic, had the authority to override decisions or appointments taken by the collective body? In other words, if there was a decision that was adopted by a majority, could he override it by virtue of his position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm going to object to that question as leading. Obviously, we're now beginning to get into more core areas of the testimony concerning Mr. Prlic's function. I think an open question is, "Can you describe Mr. Prlic's function," without leading the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't want to go into that specific detail, but I'll go about it another way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was the function of the president of the HVO HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: According to our organisation, they were involved in different fields. I was involved in the organisation of finance. I prepared regulations, proposals for appointments and so on. I sent them to the office of the president of the HVO. The president of the HVO would set the agenda. We discussed the decisions, and after a vote was taken these decisions would be signed by the president and they would be published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about appointments to various positions?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: As for the appointment of my assistants, I would propose candidates, and just like the other decisions, the council would debate that, the council would confirm the decisions, and then the decision would be signed by the president and it would be published in the Official Gazette. If the members of the council would not agree with my proposal, then I would put forth another candidate. And I was independent in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I just want to -- concretely, though, we understand -- we have seen documents that Dr. Prlic -- bearing Dr. Prlic's signature with various appointments or decisions. Were those his appointments or were those the appointments of the collective body, the HVO HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said the proposal for my assistants would come from me, and the HVO would vote and confirm the decision. Prlic would sign it, and his office would send it to the Official Gazette to be published.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So let me make sure that I'm crystal clear. Whose appointment is it? Is it Prlic's appointment, by virtue of his signature of the document, or is it the appointment of the HVO HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've heard some testimony in the past concerning the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Perhaps you could very briefly describe to us the relationship between the Presidency, as a body, and that of the HVO HZ-HB, which is the executive authority.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: From the very outset, the relationship between the Presidency and the HVO HZ-HB was a conflicting one, in a way, in terms of its content. In the Presidency of the HVO HZ-HB, there were the presidents of the municipal HVOs that were supposed to implement the decisions that were made by the HVO. On the other hand, they adopted these decisions and they assessed the work of the HVO. In the stage when the implementation would start, the implementation of the decisions of the HVO, basically most of the resistance came from the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just for correction on the record, it may be a mis-translation or it may be that Mr. Tomic misspoke, but on page 32, line 5, there's a reference to the Presidency of the HVO HZ-HB. I don't think there was any such body, if he's talking about the Presidency of the HZ-HB. Perhaps that can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, don't worry about what's on the transcript. If you could just clarify at this point, was there a Presidency of the HVO HZ-HB or was there a Presidency of the HZ-HB? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Presidency of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Occasionally, mistakes are made, and we try to clarify them, so don't be surprised if there's some interventions. And we appreciate Mr. Scott's intervention in this case. Now, we also heard that Mate Boban was the president of the Presidency as well as the president of the HZ-HB. If you could kind of clarify his position and his relationship between -- with the Presidency as well as with the HVO HZ-HB, the executive authority.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Since the defence of the area started earlier on, that is to say, before the HZ-HB was established, Mr. Boban was practically president of the HZ-HB and commander of the HVO at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. It says here: "Before the HZ-HB was established, Boban was practically the president of the HZ-HB." Are you -- so can you please clarify that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. That's the executive authority?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. The answer of the witness was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I see that. It is kind of disruptive of the flow of the testimony, but we have to do it this way, and I apologise. Perhaps it's -- it's Monday morning, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is a distinction between HVO HZ-HB and the Presidency of the HZ-HB; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes. The Presidency of the HZ-HB was the legislative body and the HVO HZ-HB was the executive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue where we were talking about Mr. Boban. Just a point of clarification. Again so that we all understand, because it says in the transcript that the HZ-HB was the executive, and I understand that maybe the gentleman is not recording everything in the transcript, but at some point the transcript will be clarified. There is the HVO HZ-HB, that's the executive, and then there is the Presidency of the HZ-HB; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. The Presidency is the legislative --

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The HVO HZ-HB is the executive?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now that we've clarified that, if you could please tell us Mate Boban's function prior to your involvement with the HVO HZ-HB, this executive authority.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Mate Boban was president of the HZ-HB and president of the Presidency of the HZ-HB. That is to say, he was the president of the legislative authority, and at the same time he was the main commander of the HVO as the military structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were appointed, by whom were you appointed? This is, I believe you said, April 15, 1992. Who appointed you? Or August, I'm sorry, August. I apologise. August 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The decision on my appointment was signed by Mr. Mate Boban, president of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how is it that you were appointed to this position?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The state of war went on for a while, and in the area under HVO control the municipalities took power, established various points and institutions that functioned earlier on in the area and that were of a regional or a republican character seized to function, so at that moment the Presidency of the HZ-HB passed a decision on the establishment -- or, rather, the appointment, I'm sorry, the appointment of Mr. Prlic as president of HVO, as the executive authority, and I was appointed head of the financial department. Our task was to try to organise civilian life, as it were. Schools were supposed to start working shortly, universities, and institutions that were financed or, rather, institutions that were supposed to finance them did not exist because they had been financed regionally or from the republican budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to slowly get into this in more detail, but first: We have come across some documentation that prior to your appointment as the head of the finance department, that position was held by Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us whether, when you inherited this position, whether you found anything in place, any legal instruments that might have been drafted, actions that had been taken, prior to that; prior to your appointment, that is?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: As I was appointed to this position, I didn't find any papers or any people or any premises that would belong to the finance department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you please describe to us, then, what sort of legal instruments were available at the time of your appointment? And we have seen the statutory decision, for instance. Aside from that, can you please explain to us what sort of legal instruments you inherited that would give you an indication of what your functions and those of other members of the HVO HZ-HB were?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: At the time, we could see the statutory decision that defined the duties of the department. The Presidency of the HZ-HB had passed that decision. As for the legislation that was available at the time, for the most part these were laws of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that had been passed in March 1992 and that had mostly been taken over from the former Yugoslav laws regulating the field of finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, here's how we're going to proceed, Mr. Tomic and Your Honours: For the next segment, I'm going to ask you to briefly describe to us, you know, how it is that you went about establishing the priorities of your department. Then we're going to look at what was occurring at the municipal level, the various municipalities. And then we'll get into the documents that are related to the HVO HZ-HB, particularly in your field. So that's to give everybody an idea of where we're going. So, first, if you could explain to us, now that you have been appointed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. A small detail. You said that you succeeded Mr. Prlic in the finance department, but you added this. You said, "I found no document. I found no civil servant and no offices, so I wondered what Mr. Prlic was doing." Could you clarify this? Since you succeeded someone, did that person -- or had that person not done anything at all? And if he had, you didn't come across any documents, you didn't meet the people he worked with, and you didn't come across any office he might have been in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic was appointed on the 15th, on the 15th of May, as head of the finance department. However, at the time he was in Mostar, and he worked in the special-purpose council as coordinator. As far as I know, he took part, as head of the finance department, in the preparation of the session of the Presidency of the HZ-HB that was held at the time when my appointment was carried through. What he did and what he wrote was from home. I mean, there were no offices, there were no premises for the finance department, and there was no staff either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I have understood correctly, you headed this department, this was in August, but this department was not structured or organised, had no staff, and you had to do everything. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's talk about what -- the priorities that you set and how you went about establishing the functions of the Department of Finance. Could you please tell us, what were the sort of things that you were looking at, as far as establishing, to start off with, and how did you go about carrying out your tasks?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: As I often travelled as a member of the special-purpose council, I went through different areas and I saw that all municipalities had turned their areas into customs areas, taxation areas. Check-points were placed where customs duty was collected, and taxes too. After the Yugoslav customs service broke up, a republican service was not established. The public accounting service, the SDK, also -- was also in disarray. There was no communication. The Revenues Administration, which had also been organised through a republican institution, was cut off from Sarajevo, and it was reduced to municipal organs. So on the whole, chaos prevailed and there were individualised solutions according to different municipalities. Municipalities financed defence, and those that were not involved in war operations were richer municipalities and they could afford better salaries. Soldiers from other municipalities did not receive salaries at all because there was no economic activity. And I could see what the situation was on the ground. Then I prepared a set of regulations that should be passed as soon as possible, a minimum of regulations for the field of finance, in order to create resources for defence that could be distributed more equitably and in order to enable the functioning of civilian institutions that were financed before the war from regional or republican levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you here for a second. Can you list, first of all, as a general principle, can you list for us what sort of priorities did these regulations have? How did you -- what were you concerned with, first of all, and then moving down the list of priorities, you being a technocrat and, in particular, being well aware of revenue collection and revenue distribution?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The first priority was the establishment of the Customs Administration, because that is a source of data for subsequent taxation, as most of the merchandise was imported. Then there was the establishment of the SDK service to provide a clearance system to avoid -- in order to avoid tax fraud. Then the establishment of the budget of the HZ-HB, to collect revenues necessary for the financing. These three institutions -- or, rather their functioning required the functioning of other institutions. However, to establish a tax administration in Mostar, before the war in Mostar there was a branch office of the Yugoslav Tax Administration. Five staff were left, three Croats and two Bosniaks, and we were supposed to create a customs administration with these five people. We had to pass regulations, find staff, train them and get going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to take it step by step. We're going to take it step by step here. Let's start off with -- you said the priorities were customs, SDK, budget. Those were the three big-ticket items, so let's start off with customs. First of all, why was it necessary to establish the Customs Administration, to start off with?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the customs database was the basis for subsequent taxation and monitoring the economy in the area controlled by HZ-HB, as there was practically no domestic manufacturing, no production. At that time, on the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, there were no customs bodies because the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not established a customs administration. There was an attempt by the Yugoslav Customs Administration, when Slovenia and Croatia declared independence, there was an attempt to draw a border between Siroki Brijeg and Mostar and raise customs duties there. That was supported by the JNA during their -- while they were still in Mostar. So there was no customs administration, but we needed one to create the preconditions for a budget and for tax control and supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, is the collection -- the establishment of a customs authority at the border, the collections of customs and maybe the imposition of a tariff system, are those not the functions of a state as opposed to a region or municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course that is a prerogative of a state, and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had taken over the customs law, but there was no administration to implement it, and there were no border crossings. So at the time the municipalities started collecting taxes and customs duties that, under the law, were -- belonged to the state. But there was nobody else to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say the municipality started collecting taxes, are we talking about municipalities within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or also other communities that were outside, such as, let's say, Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: It was the case throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. Every municipality tried to raise funds, starting from customs through taxes, to which under the law the state is entitled. But due to the problem with the communications, that wasn't possible, so that they kept that revenue to themselves and they passed municipal regulations that turned that revenue into municipal revenue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we are now dealing with a very complex and very technical issue, but you seem to be a specialist of this matter. That's why my question is going to be extremely specific. Under the former regime, under the Yugoslav regime, what about the municipalities' budgets? Was it a matter that the federal state was dealing with or a matter that came under the republic? In 1989, what about the budget of the Mostar municipality? Did it come under the federal government, the republican government, or the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The budget was adopted by the municipality, but the municipal revenue was regulated by regulations at federal level, the level of the republic and the municipal level. And there was a social agreement in place about taxation policy, and there was federal tax. At the level of the republic, there was a law regulating the subject matter of taxation and stipulating which part of the tax belonged to the municipality. For example, sales tax were divided between the municipality and the republic, so that the revenues were regulated both by republic laws and municipal regulations. The municipality wasn't in a position to collect taxes, but that mostly applied to smaller-scale taxes such as property taxes, real estate taxes, taxes on copyright fees and the like. The greatest portion of the revenue stemmed from sales tax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Once the federal state stopped existing when Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina became independent, these federal taxes were not collected anymore, and as a result the transfer from the federal budget to the municipal budgets stopped, was stopped. You're saying, "Yes," by nodding your head, but that's not enough. Please say it clearly so that it can be recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under those circumstances, the municipalities found themselves in dire straits because some of the revenue they had before they did not receive anymore. What about the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? When you took up your position, was money transferred from the republican budget to the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main tool in the collection of taxes and the flow of money was the SDK. When the SDK fell apart and the telecommunication lines broke down, it was no longer possible to implement the existing laws and regulations, because it was impossible to transfer money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of this specific situation, you were forced to set up a new system to enable the municipality to survive, financially speaking, and that's why you explained that a customs department was set up and the SDK was revamped because it was not working anymore, and you also had to work on the budget of a municipality. So if I understand correctly, you had to set up a new system from scratch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction. At the time of the collapse of the system, the municipalities that had control of their territory and could work were actually more prosperous than before the war, because there was no transfer of money to the budget of the republic, as the SDK didn't work. But the institutions such as the pension fund, the fund for higher education from which the universities were financed, or water management which were run from the level of the republic and from where money for the pensioners came and for healthcare, they were left without money. And the municipalities continued to raise funds that they were entitled to, but they used them exclusively for defence, so that university teachers were left without salaries, secondary school teachers were left without salaries because those schools were financed from the regional level, doctors and hospitals, which were also financed from regional funds or partly from the funds of the republic, were left without salaries. So a huge number of the population or a huge part of the population was left without money. So it was our role, first and foremost, to help the citizens and the municipalities which, due to the war activities, were left without money for financing their tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, if you had not set up this customs administration, chaos, anarchy, would have ensued. Would we be right in thinking so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the ground, there was already chaos. We were trying to gain control over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a couple of points of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Prior to the breakup of Yugoslavia, was there a border control and a customs administration between the Republic, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, I guess, the Socialist Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: There were no borders. The borders were more of an administrative nature. You could see them only on maps. But in real life, there was no border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated to one of my earlier questions that this was a state function, that is, the establishment of a customs administration and the collection of customs, and I take it by that, by that answer, the monies should have been transferred to Sarajevo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And assuming that the money was capable of arriving at Sarajevo, and you've already told us that that wasn't possible, what was Sarajevo obligated to do with that money or part of the money?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo was supposed to a budget of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and part of that money would have returned to other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina to finance the institutions I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you talked about -- you used the word "fund" and "funds," and since we're on the issue of budget, are we to assume that the budget was sort of a line-item budget, where you could see how much, where, the money is supposed to be allocated to when the budget is adopted?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when you talk about funds, could you just please give us a brief description of what is a fund and how it works?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: In the transitional period in Yugoslavia, there were socialist self-management communities of interest which, in the reform processes initiated, should have become funds. These were para-budgetary institutions that had their own revenue, and in the practice we called that revenue "contributions." So there was a pension fund contribution, and there was the socialist self-management community of interest for pension insurance. They had their organisation, and it was in charge of disbursing pensions. They had their own budget and their assembly. That assembly was made up of representatives of the pensioners, on the one hand, that is, the beneficiaries, and representatives of companies, as those that were obliged to pay these contributions. All those assemblies of the republics SIZs, and there was several SIZs such as the pension SIZ, the water management SIZ, the higher education SIZ. Some of them were at regional levels, such as secondary education, others at municipal level, such as the primary education SIZ and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, was it possible, during this period of time, for the various municipalities to go into the various funds and actually collect, directly from the fund, the monies that were owed to them, monies that they had paid into the system or monies that the system was supposed to distribute to them? Would that have been possible?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: When the system collapsed, these services that managed those funds also disappeared. The municipalities passed regulations under which contributions to all these funds and taxes were turned into municipal revenue. So those monies were not transferred to the accounts of those SIZs or funds because there was no clearing system and services were not paid. Secondary schools, higher education, did not function, pensions were not paid out, so that the municipalities imposed a synthetic rate of 80 per cent or even 100 per cent of the net salary to direct those monies into their budgets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You might need to explain that a little bit to us. When you say "a synthetic rate," I think I understand you, but what exactly are you saying, aid, 100 per cent? Is that a contribution?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: So if we take the net salary of an employee, taxes and contributions were calculated on the basis of that net salary. That was the system that was in place. The taxes were the revenue of the municipality and the republic. They were divided. And the contributions would go to the SIZs: 20 per cent for pension insurance, 15 per cent for healthcare, primary education, 5 per cent. So the total of all those -- all those contributions and taxes amounted to about 80 to 100 per cent of the net salary. Companies paid some additional contributions that were linked to their income or profit, but speaking about salaries, the total rate was about 80 per cent because there was a campaign in place to reduce general expenditures. Municipalities that had all those taxes and contributions put together in one rate would continue collecting all those, but they would put all that money -- direct all that money into their budgets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, going -- let's move on to the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Under the former socialist regime, when someone received a salary, would that person have to pay taxes on that salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A worker would get his net salary, and the taxes and contributions were paid by the company where that worker was employed, so that the worker, personally, never -- would never know how much tax was paid on his salary or the total of the contributions. Only if a worker had a large income, they, at the end of the year -- he or she would have to pay additional tax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
