utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand properly, under the former socialist system employees would receive a net salary, except for those who received a much higher salary. But when you, yourself, set up a new system, things were different. People received a gross salary and then had to pay various taxes, so that in the end, if I understand correctly, people -- some people would have to pay about 80 per cent of their salary in various taxes, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there is a misunderstanding. Workers would always get a net salary, so -- and that salary was transferred to their current account, and the taxes or contributions would be calculated by the company based on the net salary. And the total of those taxes and contributions would amount to a total of about 80 per cent in relation to the net salary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take the case of someone working for the municipality in Mostar, a garbage collector. Under the former regime, under the federal regime, or under the new regime, the new system, the salary of this particular employee was not taxed. It was up to the employer to pay various taxes and contributions. The employee would receive exactly the same pay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the net salary principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it the difference now between -- under the old -- prior to the war, the conflict, was the money at one point -- prior to the conflict, the money would be directed to Sarajevo, and then it would be distributed from Sarajevo to the various municipalities, whereas now, as I understand your testimony, the municipalities are keeping the money for themselves and not sending it on to Sarajevo, and then taking care of their particular needs. Is that how we are to understand your direct testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next priority, you indicated the SDK -- the SDK, that's a system that you spoke about earlier. Can you please explain to us what exactly you did or your department did to make this function?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: First, we passed regulations governing the work of our organisation, and then started to renew the network and establish communication between the offices of the SDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how far were you able to establish the offices? And in relation to that question, were you able to link up, as it were, with Sarajevo? And if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: In most of the municipalities, the offices were physically intact. Mostar was a problem because the building and all the equipment were left on the -- in the eastern part of town and was destroyed. Then we found other premises for what was to become the central branch for calculations and analyses of financial flows. We were able to procure the same kind of equipment as the one that was used before the war by the SDK of the republic and software from the head office in Sarajevo. Thus, we were able to get Mostar running. The greatest problem was that of the phone lines, but by the end of the year we were able to solve that. We did not have communication with Central Bosnia, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And two questions. One: Were you ever able to solve the issue of communications with Sarajevo so that you could link up with the Sarajevo SDK, the central government?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Technically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, secondly, you said that you were able to get the software from Sarajevo. Two questions. One: Why was the software necessary? Presumably, the SDK was functioning prior to the conflict and where the entire country was linked into the system, so why was it necessary to get software? And, number 2, and perhaps even more importantly, how is it that the software came to Mostar from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: First of all, we needed the software that would do the operations of the central unit which was in Sarajevo and now it had to perform the same kind of work in Mostar. We decided to get the software from Sarajevo because we thought it was just a provisional solution and that soon enough we would be able to communicate with Sarajevo and that it would be easy to take it from there. The government commissioner who left Sarajevo, he was the director of the central unit in Sarajevo, was our contact person, and he made it possible for us to get the disc with the software that ran those operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, you did indicate that the equipment, that would be the hardware, I take it, was located on the east side and had been destroyed, I would take it, on or about April-May 1992, so how did you deal with the issue of the hardware, if that was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, the hardware was specific, because Bosnia and Herzegovina used NCR equipment. It was actually on its way out, becoming obsolete. Croatia and Slovenia no longer used this equipment in their systems, so that we were able to find this software [as interpreted] in Slovenia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, "hardware."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and we were able to use the same equipment throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. And, finally, we have ten minutes left before our lunch break, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait, wait, I'd like to go back to a minor issue maybe, but which is essential to me. That software you mentioned, you said that you asked the Sarajevo representative, who was the director of the unit in charge of that software, to give it to you. Does it mean that the Sarajevo authority had given the go-ahead or was it given to you in an official manner? Did you receive it via personal contact with that individual or did you obtain the software in a very official manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commissioner was an official, and we requested that assistance be given to us to be able to perform this kind of operation, because we didn't have communications with Sarajevo, and he arranged for us to get this disc when an employee of the SDK in Sarajevo managed to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina knew about this. They were aware that that disc had been given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, did you have a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I was just wondering, "was given to you," was given to the municipality of Mostar, is that correct, or was given to HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was passed for the SDK HZ-HB because this is the kind of software that can be only used in the central offices of the SDK, not in the municipal branches, because this is the software that brings together the work of various branch offices, it analyses the data, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in the remaining minutes, if we could quickly cover the third aspect of your priorities, which was the budget, because that was the third thing that you indicated. If you could briefly describe to us, why was this necessary? And perhaps even more importantly, what exactly did you envisage as far as putting together the budget for HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: One of the key reasons why the budget was passed was to ensure the transparency in the way in which public revenue was used, so we had to adopt a budget, we had to define what revenues were in the budget, went into the budget, what outlays were to be financed from the budget, because it was very important, in terms of assuming the powers that in the meantime had been carried out by the municipalities, they enforced it in their areas, and we had to show that we would be able to finance areas that were of common interest, and that this was not just a matter of us taking the money from the municipalities, but of us providing services that used to be financed at the republican regional levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It sounds a little bit like the accusations made against Barak Obama, spreading the wealth around, collecting the money from the various the municipalities and then spreading it to the various areas on an on-need basis. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, more or less, because the municipalities of Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, Ljubuski, Livno, Duvno, Posusje were able to get the revenues, whereas for instance Mostar, Stolac, partly Capljina, to say nothing about other municipalities such as Kupres, were simply not in a position to have any kind of economic activity in their territory and they could not collect any revenue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So we're talking about, and correct me if I'm wrong, is trying to establish, through your budget, a single economic space within the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just very briefly, I think I can fire off two or three more questions before we break. Looking at the three priorities, customs being the first one, I take it with customs goes the tariff system, or is that separate?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Customs requires a decision on the organisation of the customs service, the law on customs with the appropriate tariffs which are a part thereof, so these are the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about -- when you talk about the SDK and establishing a budget, were efforts made concerning, for instance, a tax system, or did you adopt simply the old system that was in existence?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: At this stage, a system that was being established was the one that was in line with the regulations adopted by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so for the most part this was a reconstruction of the old system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And perhaps this might be a good time to break, and when we return, I'll be asking you about banking and insurance, before we go into what happened in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good morning to Your Honours, although I haven't had a chance to address you, except very briefly. Good morning to you and good morning to counsel and all those in the courtroom. If we could just -- I don't think I have to say anything -- well, perhaps out of an abundance of caution, we should go into private session for a moment, because I know the Chamber's had a view about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're back in open session. We'll have our lunch break until 1.00, and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, Mr. Karnavas -- or Mr. Registrar, rather, told me you had used one hour and fifty-three minutes, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Registrar, do you have IC numbers to give us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Stojic Defence has submitted a list of documents to be tended through witness Simunovic, Marinko. The list will be given Exhibit number IC 00874. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in and around the courtroom. I trust everybody had a lovely lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tomic, let's pick up where we let off, and I said that I would briefly ask you about banking and insurance, whether any efforts were made concerning those two items while you were part of the -- while you were the head of the Department of Finance. So could you please explain to us whether any efforts were made in those two areas?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Those were two very important areas, given the conditions under which Bosnia-Herzegovina became independent, important both for the communication with the world and for the economic system. Banking in the territories that are part of the HZ-HB were -- was falling apart. No bank had its corporate headquarters there. They had their corporate headquarters in Sarajevo or Zagreb, Belgrade, Split, and no bank had its corporate headquarters in HZ-HB. That was a huge problem for payment, for receiving money from abroad, and it was a problem for both companies and individuals, most of all for pensioners who had earned their pensions abroad, in Germany or Austria, for example. Talking about insurance, the situation was the same there. The insurance companies had their corporate headquarters in Sarajevo or Belgrade, Zagreb; whereas in Mostar and in the area of HZ-HB, they only had branch offices, that is, organisational units with no legal personality. Another problem with insurance existed until Bosnia-Herzegovina became a member country of the Green Card organisation, which has -- or, rather, the member states of which are entitled to issue the car insurance green card which is valid in all member countries and makes it possible for trucks and automobiles to drive on the roads of those countries. For those reasons, the companies in HZ-HB opened accounts with banks in Croatia or Slovenia. Those were non-resident accounts, based on the pertinent agreement between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other country, so all the insurance actually came from those banks. And we passed regulations to the effect that in the area of HZ-HB, those banks can operate that are registered in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That way, we practically closed down the branch offices of Zagrebacka Banka, Privredna Banka Zagreb, Splitska Banka, and made them establish new banks in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in line with Bosnia-Herzegovinian legislation. And those banks could also do business with partners abroad, provided they have an agreement of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The former branch offices that were active in the area of HZ-HB could either get together and establish a new insurance company or, alternatively, insurance companies from other countries could come in. In this case, insurance companies from Croatia. That was crucial for the circulation of people and goods because nobody could actually travel abroad in their own vehicles. Only trucks with Croatian or Slovenian license plates could enter Bosnia-Herzegovina, but ours could not go to those countries because they didn't have a green card. Due to the understanding of the green card office, national green card office of Croatia, and the efforts of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian authorities, a transitional solution was found for -- with regard to this problem with the green card, so that Bosnia-Herzegovinian insurance companies could use the green card issued by a company from Croatia. These could be affiliated companies or they would -- they could be -- there could be a different relationship between them. But, anyway, a solution was necessary to provide conditions for civilised and normal life in HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could just, to put it in a more concrete fashion so we all understand it, I believe I -- I think I got the gist of this, but perhaps you could tell us, Sarajevo, how did -- whether Sarajevo made some sort of arrangements to have green cards being able to issued, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The system of issuing green cards was not organised by Sarajevo. It was organised as a result of the talks between representatives of the BiH government in Zagreb and us, who tried to find a solution with the green card office in Zagreb, a solution which would be in line with the international regulations governing green cards. The insurance companies from Sarajevo, such as Zojl, actually applied the same motto as we did in HZ-HB. Zojl actually used the green card issued by the insurance company Mediteran from Ploce. Croatian insurance from Ljubuski would use the green cards issued by Croatian insurance, Zagreb; and Euroherc would use the green card of a Croatian insurance company from Makarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any questions from the Bench, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas, as you invite us. I would like you to explain what the relationship to the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in this, because you have told us that you had contact with Croatian banks provided there was an agreement with the National Bank of Sarajevo. Could you explain why it was necessary to have such an agreement and what role the National Bank played at that time, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the law on the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina and on the banking system in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to found a bank you need the approval of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in addition to meeting all the other requirements of that law. So the approval of the National Bank is required for any bank to be internationally acknowledged and to be licensed to take part in international -- under the international payment system, to get a Swift code, et cetera. The National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, due to the wartime conditions and the disruption of the communications lines, was only carrying out part of its -- part of its activities. We still had the -- the national currency still had not been introduced, and much data was lost due to the collapse of the SDK system, so the activities of the National Bank were reduced to a minimum and mostly limited to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. But there was contact and you had some contact with the National Bank to authorise the creation of new branches of Croatian banks as banks in Herceg-Bosna, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The branches of Croatian banks had stopped operating. The Croatian banks that had operated in Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as Privredna Banka, Zagrebacka Banka, Splitska Banka, Croatia Banka, established a new bank, the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Bank, and got approval for that. The former branch offices now became the branch offices of the new bank, and the governor of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with whom we were in contact because he did leave Sarajevo, and after -- after an inspection, he issued an approval because he had seen that the requirements of the Banking Act had been met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to get back to the green card issue. My system -- sorry. My question would only be meaningful if you, yourself, owned a car. Did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did have a car at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you don't have a car which belongs to you with a green card?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... car, but the green card had expired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were driving around in your car, your own car, how did you proceed if you didn't have a green card anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not go to Croatia or other countries without a green card, and the insurance companies that were established in line with our regulations started issuing green cards, and with such a green card you could travel to Croatia, Slovenia, or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was your car insured, and if it was insured, with whom had you insured it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the beginning of the hostilities and the collapse of the former system, it was insured by the branch office of an insurance company in Mostar. The insurance -- the policy is valid for a year, so that toward the end of 1992 problems arose because the policies were no longer valid and you need new insurance. That's why we passed new regulations to provide for the registering of new companies, which then can issue green cards, so that in the following year all those whose car registrations had expired were again in a position to be able to go abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood properly, you were able to get a new green card, and your private car had a new registration number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We got a new insurance policy issued by a newly-established insurance company registered in the area or in the territory of HZ-HB, but cars in Tuzla could get a registration and a green card issued by Zojl following the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Zojl was able to operate because it was tied into a bank or associated with a bank in Ploce, is that correct, which is in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Zojl Sarajevo is one of the founders of an insurance company in Ploce, in Croatia, and that insurance company guaranteed for green cards issued by Zojl Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, there was a question posed about the National Bank, and at one point you said that at least at that point in time they had not issued new currency. Did there come a time, to your understanding and knowledge, that the central bank in Sarajevo issued a new currency, the Bosnian or Bosnian-Herzegovinian dinar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: In September, we received information that Sarajevo had printed money, the Bosnia-Herzegovinian dinar, and on that occasion the government commissioner from Sarajevo came to the territory of HZ-HB to organise the transportation of that money, which was printed in Celj, the transportation of that money to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And speaking to that commissioner, we insisted that one-third of that money remain on the territory of HZ-HB, which was respected. In that manner, the BiH dinar actually physically arrived to HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the translation, we hear "territory," and I believe you're using the word "area." Okay, which word are you using?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Okay, "area." Right, "area."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But let me go back to that. Why is it there was sort of an insistence that one-third of the printed money, this new dinar, remain in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? On what basis was one-third being requested to remain there?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of HZ-HB had earlier decided not to acknowledge any debts incurred by Bosnia-Herzegovina unless there is a clear link to HZ-HB, so that the same principle of one-third was applied to oil or any other aid which was arriving at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I just want to make sure that we all understand this, because -- I think I do, but maybe there's a bit of a subtlety here. We're talking about debts incurred by Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are we talking about debts throughout this period that are being incurred; in other words, the government in Sarajevo incurring debts and then trying to spread it to areas that are not benefitting from whatever the monies are coming from these debts?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: When a country takes up liabilities, then it does so with its budget, and the budget is financed from the entire area of the state. So, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did -- can you tell us whether, indeed, some monies from this new currency were left behind for the usage within the area of the HZ-HB, and if so, how much?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The money was transported in three trucks, and one truck remained in the area of HZ-HB, and the SDK received that money and put it into the safes of their branch offices at Siroki Brijeg and Posusje. Through the establishment of the SDK and the opening of accounts for companies and institutions, the accounts with the SDK were opened in BiH dinars. But due to the presence of other currencies, such as the Croatian dinar and the German mark, subordinate accounts were opened in German marks and Croatian dinars. But in HZ-HB, there was no demand for BiH dinars because all trade was -- the trade relations were with Croatian and other European countries. The BiH dinar was not worth much, and there was high inflation, so nobody was willing to sell merchandise for BiH dinars which were not freely convertible and to German marks or Croatian dinars so as to preserve value. In Central Bosnia, it was possible to use the BiH dinar, because there, as it was an isolated area, it was much easier to control the BiH dinar and its value; so that the BiH dinars that came to the area of HZ-HB, following the decisions of the HVO, was transferred to the municipalities in Central Bosnia, Travnik, Zenica, Vitez, Novi Travnik and others, which municipalities bought coal with that money and paid for food and other commodities, because the BiH dinar was used there. But in Tuzla, which was practically an island, the BiH dinar -- the value of the BiH dinar would be different, so the currencies used in HZ-HB were mostly the Croatian dinar and the German mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If there are any questions from the Bench on this. Otherwise, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- before we get into, concretely, some of the documents that relate to the HZ-HB, let's focus on some of the activity that was happening at the various municipalities, to give sort of a flavour to the Trial Chamber and to others as to what's going on at that time. So with that, let's look at -- we're going to look at first various documents that relate to Mostar municipality. We've devised them in various municipalities, as opposed to going chronological. The first document is 1D 00559, and this is a decision to transfer funds collected from taxes and contributions. We see Mr. Topic's name. This is in June 1992. Can you comment on this, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, once the payment transaction system went down in the SDK accounts, where taxes and contributions for pension insurance, health insurance, culture, were collected, those were the things that were meant to be at the republican and regional levels, the funds were there, but now the municipality took over the role of the republic and orders that those funds be transferred into its own accounts for the purpose of its own budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00560. 1D 00560. This is a decision on the rate of personal income tax and contributions. Again, it's from Mr. Topic. It's dated 5 June 1992. Very briefly, can you comment on this and tell us whether this, prior to the conflict, whether this would have been a municipal function or a function carried out at the state level?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Here, the municipality takes upon itself the role of the former socialist self-management communities of interest and funds in the republic and sets a unique rate for taxes and contributions to be levied on the salaries. And we have an arbitrary rate set here at 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00561. 1D 00561.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. So that I'm sure I understand correctly, at rates of 100 per cent, does that mean that there is an imaginary salary sum at the company for an employee, let's say a thousand. Of these thousand, 500 are taxed and the rest is paid, so that the tax paid is 100 per cent of the salary -- the net salary? Is this what the 100 per cent means or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You have the salary that is paid out to the worker, and then you have another salary, so to speak, which is then paid in the form of taxes and contributions into those funds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And taking up that question, if I just -- to make sure that we understood your earlier testimony, from that 100 per cent that would be for the contribution, at least in the old system, then that would be divided into various percentages that would go into various funds to cover insurance, hospitalisation, and so on and so forth; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. That's how it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00561, the same time, and this is a decision on the allocation of basic and special sales tax on goods and services, and again can you just very briefly -- it talks about a war budget. Just very briefly comment on that.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, pursuant to this decision, it is ordered then that basic and special taxes should be paid into the accounts of the Mostar municipality. The situation was such that they were paid into the Sarajevo account, and then Sarajevo paid back 25 per cent of it to the municipality. And now the municipality collects all this revenue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00573, 26th June 1992, a decision on the conditions of sales of goods. Can you comment very briefly on that? If you look at Article 4, for instance, the sale tax shall be paid in the currency in which the goods were purchased or sold. Is that usual?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, this is yet another makeshift solution and an attempt to regulate trade. In this case, we're talking about Mostar. Of course, sales tax is paid in the currency that is the legal tender in the state, and then this decision would indicate that it could be paid in BH dinars, in Croatian dinars, in dollars, in German marks. The decision itself was quite ineptly drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00581. This is 1D 00581. This is a decision on the introduction of the Croatian dinar as a means of payment in Mostar municipality. And if we could focus our attention, for instance, to save time, on Article 2. If you could comment on that.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, as a consequence of the openness of the market and procurement from Croatia, and the large amount of cash that came in through the refugees whose families had found accommodation in Croatia, the Croatian dinar gained prevalence, and here it is introduced as a means of payment for cash transactions, not when payments were made into the accounts. So at this time, other currencies were also acceptable. It was not exclusively Croatian dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00597. 1D 00597, 25th July 1992. This is a decision on the temporary ban on payment of salaries and other income to workers employed by legal entities and other persons. And again just -- I know you're familiar with these documents, so if you could concentrate on perhaps Articles 4 and 5 and give us an opinion.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: This decision is again ineptly drafted, because it puts a ban on legal entities operating by effecting payments from one account to another in other countries where there are employees working for that company in those countries, so it cannot be implemented at all. But Article 5 is, in fact, a bigger problem in this decision, because it is indicated here that the ban shall last until the members of the Mostar municipal HVO have been paid. This is probably the reason why it was passed. The soldiers were not getting paid. And then a ban was placed on paying salaries to others. In previous decisions, we saw that the taxes and contributions levied on the salaries were, in fact, the source for the funds for the municipal budget, where the soldiers would actually be paid from, so this is a contradictory decision and probably was there for its psychological effect at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So, in other words, until the soldiers got paid, these employees are not getting paid? That's what this means?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But they still have to work, I take it.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02002, if you could look at that document, sir. Oh, I'm sorry, I skipped one document. That would be 1D 00605, 605. It's a decision on the -- a change on the decision of the introduction of the Croatian dinar. And we see from Article 1 that the prices -- all participants in cash transactions are obliged to set prices and exhibit them in Croatian dinar or Yugoslav dinar. At that time, was the Yugoslav dinar still being circulated, and if so, how much of value did it have, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: This decision was passed 25 days after the decision indicating that prices could also be listed in Croatian dinars, and now we have this new "or" clause. Prices could be listed in Croatian dinars or Yugoslav dinars. There still was some Yugoslav dinar cash in circulation, but because of the inflation it was basically worthless, and prices had to be listed both in Croatian dinars and in Jugo dinars, according to the old regulations. But because of inflation, the prices changed every day, so this was a decision enabling the shops to decide whether they wanted to list the prices in Croatian dinars or in Jugo dinars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have just seen a series of decisions taken by Mr. Topic, the president of the Municipality of Mostar. I have a question which runs as follows. Maybe you can answer it. For instance, if we look at this document, the last one we've seen, in future the transactions must be made in Croatian dinars. Why was this decision not taken by the Presidency of the HZ-HB, and even by the executive authority, the HVO? Why is it that the municipality that intervenes in an area in which it is not sovereign -- I don't understand why the municipality is passing a series of decisions which could, of course, be taken by the Presidency or the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO of the HZ-HB at this time had not been established yet. The municipalities took upon themselves all the powers and passed decisions, depending on the situation. That sometimes also had to do with the currency, for instance. And why the Presidency? Well, I really don't have an answer for you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you can't answer this question, why the Presidency did not legislate, since this body had legislative authority. Why is it that Mr. Tomic [as interpreted] took these decisions at a municipal level? "Topic," I said, not "Tomic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time the HVO had not been established yet. The finance department had not been established yet, was not operational. The municipalities were trying to deal with this on their own, trying to find their own solutions, and later on, once the HVO was established, it issued regulations pertaining to this sphere in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, during that period in which the HVO had not been established or was not operating, the municipalities held both legislative and executive powers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just so we're not -- we don't get confused months from now or years from now, when we're talking about HVO, we're talking about HVO HZ-HB, executive?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, also the Presidency that you spoke of, you did mention this earlier, but the members of the Presidency are, indeed, the presidents of these municipalities, are they not?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The presidents of the municipal HVOs were members of the Presidency, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Also keeping this -- keeping it in context and perspective, this is July 1992. What other choices, if any, were available to municipalities, such as Mostar, when it came to these sorts of issues relating to currencies, for instance?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: At that time, the only option available was to accept and to use either the Croatian dinar or the German mark, because they were present there. The German mark was present because of the large number of guest workers who worked in Germany, Austria, France, and were originally from Western Herzegovina. Some of them still worked and remitted their income back to their families in German marks or received their pensions in German marks. And as for the Croatian dinars, they were present because of the refugees who had their families in Croatia and a great deal of trade. This kind of makeshift solution is present in areas of the municipalities Capljina all the way down to Jablanica. So simply this is a result of an effort to make due in the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the last document on this -- on Mostar, which is 1D 02002, and this is not a municipal document, but this is a document by the board -- the members of the board of managers of a particular holding company, and they issue a decision, we could see that it's 3 August 1992. If we look at the last page -- the second page in English, we see, out of eight members, three have signed and one seemed to have been present at the time. And in looking at this decision, can you please give us a brief comment so that we can understand what is happening now at -- what companies are doing during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an example of how companies tried to make due in those times. Immediately before the war broke out, there was this process of ownership transfer. Social ownership was transferred into private ownership and other kinds of ownership, and various new companies were set up in accordance with the new rules. And here we can see this was a holding company, and of course this process of ownership transfer was done in a socialist manner, so to speak. Workers, employees, were able to buy equity from their salaries, equity in the company. Of course, it was a game, because their salaries would be increased to that amount, the amount that then was used for them to buy shares. But once the war broke out, there was no decision, no decree that was to be passed by a republican authority regarding the ownership transfer, to either say, "Put a stop to the ownership transfer," or to provide a model for it. And here managers, members of the board of directors, decided to put a stop to this ownership transfer process because it was no longer possible to control the inflation, salaries were not being paid; and if we're talking about this holding, it operated in the territory of several municipalities, and each municipality had its own system of running the economy and they virtually took over the company's operating as part of this holding so that the holding no longer served any purpose. And the members of the board of directors who could meet at that time made this decision, and at the same time they had lost the premises, some of the documents; and this was a makeshift solution that could be implemented at that time. But this also shows that there was this desire to protect the property at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So I think what I'm hearing is that the intentions were correct on their part, their intentions.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But was this a proper way of doing things? Did they have the authorisation to do such a thing, for instance, if we're going to go legally speaking?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I said that the republic did have power over that, but it failed to pass regulations to deal with the process of ownership transfer in the state of war or imminent threat of war, so this decision was based on the conditions, the circumstances, and this intention to protect the property of this company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you're not answering my question. My question is very direct. I understand that their intentions were good. I understand that the republic failed to do certain things. But my question is very simple. Did they have authorisation to carry out such a decision?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, as far as this particular holding company, you know, how many employees at one time did Apro have, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Before the war, when Mostar had about 50.000 employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you know whether Mr. Prlic was involved in any way with Apro, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, just before the war, was the chairman of the holding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another municipality and see what is going on in Livno. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Let us stay with the A pro holding for a moment, because what you said is of the utmost interest for me. As I understood it, there was a transition, a shift from public ownership to private ownership, and the employees of the companies became owners. Now, how could they be owners? Were they changed into owners by having their wages increased? Is this a general principle that was applied to all state or public companies that were somehow privatized by having them changed into private companies? Were all companies subject to this mechanism of shift from public to private ownership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the process of the ownership transfer or transformation, the employees had the right to buy the shares first, and they decided how much -- how many of the shares in their company they wanted to buy, and they were given some discounts. They could buy those shares at a discount. The employees and the managers mostly bought those shares. Managers usually bought more shares for bigger amounts of money. At that time, there was a recommendation in place by the political structures that the salaries of the employees should be increased in order to make it possible for them to buy those shares. So it was a closed circle. Of course, you didn't get the raise that corresponded to the amount of shares that you paid for the shares, but there was an across-the-board raise, pay raise, in order to speed up this process of privatization of companies and to make it possible for as many employees to actually buy those shares in their private companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, with the breakdown of the former Yugoslavia, it gave rise to a high number of small owners. Those who were wage earners, employees, they were before employees of public companies; and over night, in theory, they became owners of their own companies, is that so, as long as they could buy shares, as you said? But since they could not, a mechanism was found which was to raise their salaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was one way in which the process of the buying of shares was speeded up. This privatization was a part of the economic package introduced by Ante Markovic while he was in government. The ownership was not transferred until the moment when the employees paid the whole amount, and they actually paid it in instalments every month through their salaries. So when the war broke out, this process had not finished, and in particular in this case, it was a holding, it was a new form of corporation which was not present before, where the daughter companies of this holding were to transfer their property to the holding, and the holding was supposed to manage the property. And this process had not been completed, this process that was part of the ownership transfer, so the management here decided to put a stop to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, just one question before we move on to another municipality. I would, indeed, like to go back to the issue of taxes and contributions on personal income in the Mostar municipality. It's document 1D 00560. We saw in this document that residents in the municipality had decided that the employees would pay taxes and contributions on their income. The amount was to be earmarked to the war effort. Here's my question: Was it some kind of special levy, in addition to the contribution paid usually by citizens to the state, or was this the only contribution paid by citizens? And if it was, in the Mostar municipality did the employees pay another contribution to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina or were all links severed, so that when an employee would pay his or her contribution to the Mostar municipality, they had nothing else to pay, in terms of contribution, nothing to pay to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Taxes and contributions that were paid in respect of salaries were the only form of taxation on salaries at that moment. Later on, Mostar introduced a war tax of 10 per cent, so the 100 per cent of salaries went to the municipal budget and there were no other payments made to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because there was no way of sending that money out there. As for these 100 per cent, there is a certain part of taxes and contributions that was, indeed, supposed to go to Sarajevo, but due to the breakdown in communications and due to the fact that these services were not rendered, those that were supposed to be financed by the republic, that is, all the money was kept in the budget of the municipality of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understood your answer. So that the part was not paid to the government of BiH because there were problems in communication. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Tell us the other -- complete the process. Money can't go to Sarajevo, but once -- if it went to Sarajevo, assuming it could go there, was Sarajevo responsible for then returning some of that money back to the various municipalities, and if so, was that able -- was Sarajevo able to do that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: When taxes and contributions are paid, every one of these taxes and contributions has an account of its own at the SDK. These are the so-called transient accounts. A payment is made to these accounts, and then automatically the SDK further sends the money to the beneficiary. Now, regardless of whether it will be the republican budget, the self-management interests community, or a fund for education, higher education, health, et cetera, then all of the recipients of this money finance these services at the level of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the retirement fund sends pensions to Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, et cetera. The health fund sends salaries for doctors, nurses and so on. The fund for higher education sends payments to the universities for their work and for the salaries of the employees there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if I understand you correctly so we can just move on, essentially the money is kept at the municipal rather than being sent on, but at the same time the municipality is paying for the activities that would normally be paid from the contributions made by the state ?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, to that I'm going to object for a number of reasons. One is I didn't object for the last few minutes, but then began a series of leading questions on potentially important issues. Secondly, I'm not sure the witness can confirm that in every instance, in every municipality, no monies did or could have gone back. This is incredibly -- read the question, Your Honours. Read the question and whether this witness can -- absolutely has personal knowledge to answer that question in every instance. I suggest that he cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, do rephrases, step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Earlier, you told us that the SDK wasn't properly functioning because there was a breakdown in the telecommunications system. Do you recall telling us this in the morning?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at least with respect to the areas where -- in Herceg-Bosna, do you know whether there was a possible linkage in any of those areas in Sarajevo, while Sarajevo was under blockade, for the SDK to be linked up?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's take another example. What about Tuzla? Was Tuzla, for instance, able to be linked up at the time, to your understanding and knowledge, and you were there? Were they able to be linked up with the central SDK system in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I don't -- perhaps I misheard it or didn't hear it. Mr. Karnavas just said that Mr. Tomic was in Tuzla. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I never said that, I never said that. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then that is my objection, then. What does Mr. Tomic know about what was happening in Tuzla? Was he there during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I left -- I understand the -- I understand the technique, Your Honour, of obstructing. Let me go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on you being in country - the rest of us were not, at least the Bench, the Prosecution and some of the foreigners, but some of my colleagues were there - but you being in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, do you know whether Tuzla was connected with the SDK system in Sarajevo at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: No, it was not connected, and people from Tuzla, who came to Mostar, confirmed that. Also, it is evident from the decisions they made that there was no communication with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to get to those decisions. Now, assuming contributions were made to Sarajevo, was Sarajevo capable at the time of returning those contributions if the SDK wasn't functioning?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that the higher education, I believe, at the university, that was something that had to be paid by Sarajevo. Do you know whether Sarajevo was making those contributions to pay the salaries and for the infrastructure and upkeep of the University of Mostar, for instance, at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to Livno. 1D 00798. Let's see what Livno is to go. We'll get to Tuzla at some point, but let's do Livno first. This is an order to introduce uniform pricing and methods of payment in privately-owned catering establishments. If you look at Article 1, we see payments both in Croatian dinar and in Yugoslav dinar. Now, at the time -- you briefly spoke about this, but there was some sort of private enterprise in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and catering establishments, would that one of those forms of private enterprise?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Livno was any better off than, say, Mostar when it came to being able to control the inflationary swings of the Yugoslav dinar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Livno had no possibility whatsoever to influence that in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to 1D 00801, this is May, 29 May 1992. Again, this is Livno. This is a decree on the introduction of wartime turnover tax on goods and services. If you could please look at this and give us a very brief opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The municipal assembly, in the old system, did not have the authority to impose wartime taxes in respect of the circulation of goods and services, so this part pertained to increasing levies in the field of trade and services. The revenues were sent to the budget of Livno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then if we look at the -- towards the end of this document, we see that this is delivered to the Livno SDA branch office. That was the Muslim party in Livno, was it not? The SDA, that's the Muslim party, and this is the branch party in Livno?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to 1D 00803 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, please look at Article 4 of the document. Based on the document, it looks as though the outcome -- or the tax will be paid into gyro account 11700-840-055, held at the Livno SDK. Does this mean that the turnover tax is going to be managed by the Livno SDK? At least that's what Article 4 says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Money was paid into this account, this gyro account with the SDK of Livno, and they would be supposed to send that money to the number of the account in Livno. That is what I can see from the numbers here. That is to say that there is no circulation with Sarajevo or other municipalities. It was only within that municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps one last document before we take our break. 1D 00803. 1D 00803. This is 29 May 1992. And if we look at Article 1, it says all shops whose parent company has its headquarters outside Livno are ordered to open up a gyro account at the Livno SDK. And then if we look at Article 4, Roman numeral IV, it says: "All funds remaining after the payment of the turnover tax and taxes and contributions shall be transferred to the account of the parent company as soon as this can be done."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what Livno is doing with this particular order?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Trading companies from Sarajevo, Mostar, Tuzla, that had stores in Livno, did not have an account in Livno. The account was only at the head office of the company involved. The only possibility in Livno was to collect their daily earnings in cash and to deposit them with the SDK having the account of the parent company as the ultimate beneficiary. Now, this order states that these stores have to open their own accounts at Livno. So in these stores, there would just be a store manager, people who are not even trained to manage a bank account, and there were sales people. But this order was being issued to have them open an account where they would deposit their daily earnings, because turnover tax would be paid on the basis of that. And then in number 4 it says that the turnover tax would have to be paid, although according to the old law, it is the head office of the trading company that is supposed to do that, not the actual store. And it says that this would be transferred to the account of the parent company as soon as this can be done; that is to say, that Livno did not have communication with other SDKs, where the parents company were, Mostar, Banja Luka, Tuzla, everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understand it, it was the wish of the Bench to have a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to take the last break for today, and it will be a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. We were still on Livno. If we look at 1D 00804, if you could look at this very quickly and again give us a brief comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is Livno doing on the 19th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: This was an order to confiscate funds from all the accounts that were in Yugoslav dinars, to transfer all that money to the account of the Municipality of Livno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to 1D 00806, 1D 00806, again Livno, this is an order on transactions by a group 685, a gyro account. What is this about? You may want to focus on, say, Article 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: These economic entities, that is to say, small privately-owned shops and restaurants, were not duty-bound to have gyro accounts. Now they were being told to open gyro accounts and to operate exclusively through these gyro accounts. The municipality has no jurisdiction whatsoever over the SDK, according to the old law. They are not entitled to issue such orders to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at another municipality very quickly. This would be Siroki Brijeg, starting off with 1D 02331. This is a decision on the means of payments in the area of Siroki Brijeg, and we see from -- Article 1, and then look at Article 2 very briefly, if you could comment.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: This decision introduces the Croatian dinar as means of payment in the area of Siroki Brijeg municipality. This is one of those decisions that was passed by almost all municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, which is 1D 02332, 1D 02332, a decision on the work of the SDK, Siroki Brijeg. If you could comment on it for us very briefly. Look at Article 2 in particular.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: If we look at this decision, the municipality is practically establishing its own SDK in Siroki Brijeg, of course, based on the former branch office of the publicly accounting service, the SDK, and they say that all changes should be made in Croatian dinars, and it also says that there was no payment or communication between Siroki Brijeg and other SDK offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at 1D 02333. 1D 02333. This is a decision on the source of the budget of the Municipality of Siroki Brijeg, and if you could again comment and put it in perspective, as you have been doing.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this decision, the Municipality of Siroki Brijeg takes over the revenues that, according to law, belong to the republic, and hereby they transform them into municipal revenues, 1, 2, 3. Road taxes always went to the self-management interest community or fund that was involved in road maintenance. Only a small part of the taxes under number 2 and 3 remained in the municipality, but now they are simply being taken over by the budget of the Municipality of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Let's remain with this document, Witness. I'm curious about one thing, but I don't have the law before me, because this is a decision which is pursuant to regulation 66, paragraph 3, of the law that was published in the Official Gazette of the RBH. Now, what is this Article 66? Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it pertains to the right of municipalities to pass decisions, generally speaking, general decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because we can see that this municipality is based -- or is invoking the legislation or the law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but maybe Mr. Karnavas will have time to find Article 66 for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, and that can be found -- it's in the e-court, Your Honours, at 1D 00897. 1D 00897. And I had intended to bring it, and it was an oversight on my part. I looked at that in the office. But we can easily deal with that tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 02334, 1D 02334, this is a decision on a turnover tax on goods and services of Siroki Brijeg, and if you could comment on this. And perhaps for those of us who are not terribly familiar with the taxation system, what is a turnover tax?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Turnover tax is a tax that is paid when products are sold. There is a turnover tax on retail goods and also there is a turnover tax on wholesale goods, that is to say, when one big company is selling goods to another big company, whereas retail turnover tax is when it is the ultimate consumer who is involved in the purchase. Then this tax has to be included in the price. At any rate, this decision was made by the Municipality of Siroki Brijeg. It was supposed to be the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to pass this decision. Practically, this is the law in its entirety, in abbreviated form, though, and the tariff as well. The tariff is important because the tax is calculated on the basis of that tariff. So, for example, this tariff shows that municipalities where trade could be conducted tried to be more favourable than others, as it were. For example, in this tariff, the tax on gasoline, cigarettes, is lower than before; and the municipalities, for the most part, took over the former republican tariff. Now the Municipality of Siroki Brijeg is introducing lower rates so that their companies would be less expensive and thereby bring more revenue to the budget of the Municipality of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the final document in this batch, and that's 1D 02337, this is a decision on the control of movable goods in the area of Siroki Brijeg municipality. And focusing on Article 1, we can see it says: "Control of entry and exit of all goods in the areas of Siroki Brijeg municipality will be carried out by the relevant inspection services, with mandatory assistance by military and civilian police." And then again in Article 2, it talks about entry and exit points to and from Siroki Brijeg, you know, that they must record every invoice and all goods in transit through the area of Siroki Brijeg municipality. Could you -- and then of course you can look at Article 4 as well. But could you please give us an opinion on this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- I'm sorry, it was a rather long question, but I have a question to the previous chapter. And I wonder, Mr. Tomic, whether I understood you correctly. I seem to have heard that the Municipality of Siroki Brijeg, via the turnover taxes, also interferes with competition in giving an advantage to their own companies. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in light of that question, do you know whether other municipalities did sort of the same thing or was this unique to Siroki Brijeg at the time or even thereafter?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: That was typical of municipalities, depending on what kind of companies could be found in their area. They would try to favour them to sell as much as possible because, in return, they would get more revenue for their own budgets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I could focus your attention to the document of 1D 02337, and if you could give us a brief commentary on this particular document. Again, it's dealing with Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: In order to tax trade transactions, you need documents, and there is no customs administration in place so there is no document showing the entry of goods into Bosnia-Herzegovina or into the municipality of Siroki Brijeg. That's why this municipality of Siroki Brijeg establishes its own check-point, something of a para-custom service or a para-tax administration to introduce an entry document for commodities entering the municipality for the purpose of taxation, or in the case of transit, to know that the commodities are transiting. More or less all municipalities were doing that in order to protect their areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm a little startled by the first article. Why is this part to be played by the military police? What is the reason for that, in your view? Was it because the country was in a state of war? Why is the military police supposed to play a specific part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The state of war existed and many people were moving about with weapons, so that for the inspection to be carried out efficiently, it was necessary to protect the inspectors; and the municipalities also used those monies to pay for their own units, and they would then, in return, assist in the process of collection of revenue which was necessary for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, for the sake of time, we're going to skip over the documents dealing with the Municipality of Orasje. That would be 1D 01733 and 1D 01737, and we'll also skip over the documents dealing with Capljina, which is 1D 01111 and 1119; and let's go on to Tuzla, starting off with 1D 01374. But before we get to this document, there was an objection raised, "How would you know about what is happening in Tuzla," so just to provide us with a little bit of information right now: After the signing of the Washington Agreement -- I'm getting ahead of myself a little bit, but after the signing of the Washington Agreement, what positions did you hold?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I was appointed minister of finance of the Federation and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you were both for the Federation and for Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were both for the Federation, which that was -- which was established by the Washington Agreement, as well as for Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is Tuzla in the Federation or in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: It's in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at the time when you were involved as minister of finance for the Federation, did you have an opportunity to become acquainted with what events were going on in Tuzla concerning financial instruments during the war period, the conflict period?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I visited Tuzla personally or -- in that period, and my deputy was from Tuzla, who he was in charge of finance matters in Tuzla in the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's focus on Tuzla a little bit. We're on 1D 01374, and again we can see at the very top, at the preamble, that this is pursuant to Article 66 on the Law of All People's Defence. And, Your Honours, I'm told that if you do wish to look at that article which is in 1D 00897, it's on page 7 of the English translation, and it would be on -- and I also have the page number for the B/C/S, which is 1D 28-0440. I mean, so if Your Honours wish to ask any questions concerning that. Otherwise, I will move on. So if we look at -- if we look at this decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I have a question for the witness. You've just told us that you were the finance minister for the Federation, which is a very high-ranking position in a government. It's a very high position to be the finance minister. How long were you the finance minister for the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the first minister of finance after the Washington Treaty, and I stayed in that position up to the agreement on the creation of the Federation, that is, immediately before the Dayton Accord. And after that, I became minister of foreign trade and international communications of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that when you were appointed finance minister, you were appointed because you had special competences in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I met all conditions for that position, since I had been active in the area for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago, we talked about taxes. I was wondering if the taxes on goods and services aren't what we call in the European Union the VAT. Is it the same system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two systems of taxing turnover. In the former socialist countries, there was this one form of turnover tax applied, and in the West it was VAT. Nowadays in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have VAT also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When municipalities adopted that kind of law on taxes, I guess that they were thinking about this tax in terms of value-added tax.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Western world, it is VAT. In Bosnia-Herzegovina and former Yugoslavia, we had turnover tax, the basic difference being that turnover tax, that is, the tax on retail transactions, is paid in the final phase, whereas in VAT it is levied in every -- for every transaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at this decision, 1D 01374, this is a decision on the calculation of payment of turnover tax on goods. And if you could give us a comment on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: This decision is practically an amendment of the law on the -- on turnover tax. It says that there are no exceptions on the obligation to pay turnover tax, which tax must be calculated and paid into the account of the Tuzla budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, prior to the conflict and the seize of Sarajevo, was a municipality such as Tuzla permitted to pass a decision such as this one?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: No, municipalities could not amend laws passed at the level of the Republic, which they have done with this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 01375, this is a decision on redirecting turnover tax and goods under tariff number 8 of the schedule of basic turnover tax. If you could comment on this very briefly.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: The decision itself is titled "Decision on Redirecting," so instead of paying it into the budget of the Republic, it is paid into the budget of the Tuzla municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So going back to the question that I asked earlier, which provoked the objection: From this, can you draw any conclusions concerning the SDK and the operation of the SDK and its linkage to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Obviously, the communication lines were disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, 1D 0 -- incidentally, this gentleman, Selim Beslagic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by the name, can you tell us whether he's a Serb, a Croat, or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it while you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, granted you were in one particular area, you didn't hear about any mutiny by the Tuzla municipality against the state government in Sarajevo, where they at some point had their own sort of Boston tea party, you know, decided not to provide taxes to the state government?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: I haven't heard of anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at 1D 01396, this is an order for calculation of tax on cigarette trade. If you could give us a comment on this, and I particularly would like to know why -- what's so important about cigarette trade?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: This is also a redirection of monies levied from the tax on the turnover of cigarettes into the budget of Tuzla, under 1. And under 2, the deadline for paying turnover tax is shortened to five days. It used to be seven or fifteen days. And cigarettes are important because they are heavily taxed, and they are one of the major contributors to the budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And for the record and for everyone's convenience, if we look at the preamble, it invokes Article 39 of the Decree Law on Defence, Your Honours, in the event you wish to look that up. That's in 1D 00828, but that's the article that they're invoking for this particular order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Moving on to the next document, 1D 01399, this is an order establishing check-points for the inspection of export and import of goods, and we can -- if we look at this, we can see, especially in Article -- or Roman numeral II, check-points for inspection of exports and imports to and from Tuzla municipality which will work 24 hours a day after being established. And it talks about, in Article 5 -- Roman numeral -- I mean Roman numeral IV about the Tuzla municipal inspection service is to control it. Can you give us a comment on this?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
utterances.text: This is almost the same encounter as the decisions passed by the Municipality of Siroki Brijeg. To control the movement of commodities, the documentation must be provided to make possible a timely taxation and thus filling the budget of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just to make sure that we're crystal clear on this one, because we started off by me asking you about your initial -- how you prioritise your functions and your tasks when you were assigned to the position of Department of Finance, and you indicated customs was one of them, and when looking at this particular order, as well as the one at Siroki Brijeg, can you tell us whether it would appear that some sort of a customs system is being put in place in Tuzla and in this other municipality, Siroki Brijeg, by an order such as this?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC
